Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis
$(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$
there is a unique $R$-bilinear form
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$
with
$$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is
independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$
depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric,
$\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative,
$\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$,
where $i(a)y$ denotes the right action $y\,i(a)$ of $i(a)$ on $y$, i.e. the
left action $a\cdot y:=y\,i(a)$; (iii) characterised by
$x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for
$x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$
is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of
$x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{	imes}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ in $R$; put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{	imes}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$ ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $S_F(d,n)$-modules, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $ eta= eta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. 2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $	heta$ pullback to every Hecke module), $$\sum_{i>0} igl[S^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula is a positive filtration-sum identity expressed in a signed Weyl/Specht basis. A single nonzero signed Weyl coefficient does not force the corresponding labelled simple factor: the entire right side must first be expanded and cancelled in simple classes. For a Weyl module and an off-head label $
u$, the resulting multiplicity of $L^
u$ is an upper bound for $[W^\lambda:L^
u]$, and is positive exactly when that factor occurs in the radical. This does not give a general closed algorithm for decomposition numbers.

Fix a beta length $L\ge1$. For a partition $
u$ with at most $L$ columns (that is, $
u_1\le L$), put $$ eta_i(
u)=
u'_i+L-i\qquad(1\le i\le L).$$ Its beta numbers are strictly decreasing nonnegative integers. Conversely, from any strictly decreasing nonnegative sequence $b$ recover the unique partition with conjugate parts $
u'_i=b_i-L+i$, of degree $|
u|=\sum_i b_i-L(L-1)/2$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

For arbitrary $b\in\mathbb Z^L$, first set all its alternating symbols to zero if it has repeated entries or a negative entry. Otherwise there is a unique sorting permutation $w$ taking it to decreasing order; let $
u$ be the recovered partition and let $\epsilon(b)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$. Uniqueness of the sorting permutation is claimed only in this distinct-entry case. In the fixed degree-$r$ Grothendieck groups define $$[W^b]_{d,r}:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[W^
u],&|
u|=r	ext{ and } \ell(
u)\le d,\0,&	ext{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad [S^b]_r:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[S_{\mathrm M}^
u],&|
u|=r,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ The notation $[\Delta^b]$ is synonymous with $[W^b]_{d,r}$ when $d,r$ are fixed. The ordinary Dipper-James translation conjugates every partition label and pulls every compared module back by the same $	heta$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

For a composition $\mu$ define the signed semistandard number directly by $$d_\mu(b):= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)|T_0(
u,\mu)|,&b	ext{ has distinct nonnegative entries and }|
u|=|\mu|,\0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ Here the tableau alphabet is the length of $\mu$; a shape with too many rows automatically has no such tableau ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). This function is alternating in the beta entries. It also obeys the branching identity $$d_\mu(b)=\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\|C|=z}}  d_{ ar\mu}(b-\mathbf1_C),$$ where $z$ is the last nonzero part of $\mu$ and $ ar\mu$ deletes that part. The selected entries are **decreased by one**, not replaced by $-1$. For a decreasing beta sequence this is the deletion of the largest semistandard entries: they occupy a horizontal strip, at most one box in each selected column. Sorting extends the identity to distinct arbitrary sequences; if entries repeat, terms selecting just one of the equal entries cancel in pairs, while terms selecting both or neither vanish. Negative entries remain negative after decrementing. Thus the identity also holds in all zero-symbol cases. At $\mu=0$ its value is the sorting sign for a permutation of $(L-1,\ldots,0)$ and is zero otherwise, so the recursion terminates without another unproved extension rule.

In the formulas of this page take $L=r$ when $r>0$. A nonzero degree-$r$ partition has width at most $r$, so this length suffices; the Weyl cutoff $\ell(
u)\le d$ is retained even when $d<r$. A balanced displacement $+h\mathbf e_b-h\mathbf e_c$ preserves total degree. An unbalanced change is not silently treated as a class in the same fixed-degree group. The empty degree is handled by the empty beta sequence and unit symbol. No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S=S(d,n)$ be the
$q$-Schur algebra over $F$ with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Let $M$ be a finite
dimensional right $S$-module all of whose composition factors lie in a single
block $B$ of $S$
([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and let integers $a_{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, satisfy
$$[M]=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$$
in the Grothendieck group $G_0(S\text{-mod})$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]). Then
$W^{\lambda}$ lies in $B$ whenever $a_{\lambda}\ne0$. In particular no nonzero
virtual combination of Weyl classes all of whose terms lie outside $B$ can
equal the class of a module in $B$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then
$J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a nonzero unital ring. Then $R$ is semisimple if and only if $$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$$ for positive integers $r,n_i$ and division rings $D_i$. See [[thm-endomorphism-ring-of-the-left-regular-module-is-opposite]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

derivations.claim: Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. For $n=0$, $S_F(d,0)=F$, with its one empty-label module, so all assertions hold directly; hence assume $n>0$. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below.

Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class.

Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions.

No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition.

Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical.

The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. By [F5] and the absolute simplicity in [F1], the semisimple quotient is a product of full matrix rings over $F$. Lift its matrix diagonal idempotents: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ changes an error $a=u^2-u$ to $-3a^2+4a^3$, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_
u$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_
u=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda
u}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core.

The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Assume $e<\infty$. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, with $l=\ell(\gamma)$, and set $ho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu
eho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=ho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $
u$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $
u$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows.

Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence.

Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions.

step 2.2: equal e-cores force membership of one block, by the rim-hook induction

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis
$(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$
there is a unique $R$-bilinear form
$$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$
with
$$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is
independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$
depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric,
$\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative,
$\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$,
where $i(a)y$ denotes the right action $y\,i(a)$ of $i(a)$ on $y$, i.e. the
left action $a\cdot y:=y\,i(a)$; (iii) characterised by
$x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for
$x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$
is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of
$x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{	imes}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ in $R$; put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{	imes}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$ ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $S_F(d,n)$-modules, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $ eta= eta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. 2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $	heta$ pullback to every Hecke module), $$\sum_{i>0} igl[S^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula is a positive filtration-sum identity expressed in a signed Weyl/Specht basis. A single nonzero signed Weyl coefficient does not force the corresponding labelled simple factor: the entire right side must first be expanded and cancelled in simple classes. For a Weyl module and an off-head label $
u$, the resulting multiplicity of $L^
u$ is an upper bound for $[W^\lambda:L^
u]$, and is positive exactly when that factor occurs in the radical. This does not give a general closed algorithm for decomposition numbers.

Fix a beta length $L\ge1$. For a partition $
u$ with at most $L$ columns (that is, $
u_1\le L$), put $$ eta_i(
u)=
u'_i+L-i\qquad(1\le i\le L).$$ Its beta numbers are strictly decreasing nonnegative integers. Conversely, from any strictly decreasing nonnegative sequence $b$ recover the unique partition with conjugate parts $
u'_i=b_i-L+i$, of degree $|
u|=\sum_i b_i-L(L-1)/2$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

For arbitrary $b\in\mathbb Z^L$, first set all its alternating symbols to zero if it has repeated entries or a negative entry. Otherwise there is a unique sorting permutation $w$ taking it to decreasing order; let $
u$ be the recovered partition and let $\epsilon(b)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$. Uniqueness of the sorting permutation is claimed only in this distinct-entry case. In the fixed degree-$r$ Grothendieck groups define $$[W^b]_{d,r}:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[W^
u],&|
u|=r	ext{ and } \ell(
u)\le d,\0,&	ext{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad [S^b]_r:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[S_{\mathrm M}^
u],&|
u|=r,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ The notation $[\Delta^b]$ is synonymous with $[W^b]_{d,r}$ when $d,r$ are fixed. The ordinary Dipper-James translation conjugates every partition label and pulls every compared module back by the same $	heta$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

For a composition $\mu$ define the signed semistandard number directly by $$d_\mu(b):= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)|T_0(
u,\mu)|,&b	ext{ has distinct nonnegative entries and }|
u|=|\mu|,\0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ Here the tableau alphabet is the length of $\mu$; a shape with too many rows automatically has no such tableau ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). This function is alternating in the beta entries. It also obeys the branching identity $$d_\mu(b)=\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\|C|=z}}  d_{ ar\mu}(b-\mathbf1_C),$$ where $z$ is the last nonzero part of $\mu$ and $ ar\mu$ deletes that part. The selected entries are **decreased by one**, not replaced by $-1$. For a decreasing beta sequence this is the deletion of the largest semistandard entries: they occupy a horizontal strip, at most one box in each selected column. Sorting extends the identity to distinct arbitrary sequences; if entries repeat, terms selecting just one of the equal entries cancel in pairs, while terms selecting both or neither vanish. Negative entries remain negative after decrementing. Thus the identity also holds in all zero-symbol cases. At $\mu=0$ its value is the sorting sign for a permutation of $(L-1,\ldots,0)$ and is zero otherwise, so the recursion terminates without another unproved extension rule.

In the formulas of this page take $L=r$ when $r>0$. A nonzero degree-$r$ partition has width at most $r$, so this length suffices; the Weyl cutoff $\ell(
u)\le d$ is retained even when $d<r$. A balanced displacement $+h\mathbf e_b-h\mathbf e_c$ preserves total degree. An unbalanced change is not silently treated as a class in the same fixed-degree group. The empty degree is handled by the empty beta sequence and unit symbol. No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S=S(d,n)$ be the
$q$-Schur algebra over $F$ with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Let $M$ be a finite
dimensional right $S$-module all of whose composition factors lie in a single
block $B$ of $S$
([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and let integers $a_{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, satisfy
$$[M]=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$$
in the Grothendieck group $G_0(S\text{-mod})$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]). Then
$W^{\lambda}$ lies in $B$ whenever $a_{\lambda}\ne0$. In particular no nonzero
virtual combination of Weyl classes all of whose terms lie outside $B$ can
equal the class of a module in $B$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then
$J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a nonzero unital ring. Then $R$ is semisimple if and only if $$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$$ for positive integers $r,n_i$ and division rings $D_i$. See [[thm-endomorphism-ring-of-the-left-regular-module-is-opposite]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

derivations.claim: Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. For $n=0$, $S_F(d,0)=F$, with its one empty-label module, so all assertions hold directly; hence assume $n>0$. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below.

Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class.

Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions.

No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition.

Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical.

The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. By [F5] and the absolute simplicity in [F1], the semisimple quotient is a product of full matrix rings over $F$. Lift its matrix diagonal idempotents: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ changes an error $a=u^2-u$ to $-3a^2+4a^3$, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_
u$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_
u=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda
u}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core.

The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Assume $e<\infty$. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, with $l=\ell(\gamma)$, and set $ho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu
eho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=ho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $
u$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $
u$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows.

Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence.

Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$ and may overlap. The disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_i\{i\}\times X^{(e)}_i$ records each bead with its runner and row;
the map $(i,a)\mapsto ae+i$ bijects it with $X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$. Moreover any two normalised beta-sets
($e\mid|X|$) give the same ordered quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and weight.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For prime $e=p$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]; the same inequalities define the
extension to composite finite $e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of

two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n,0^{d-n})\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the length-$d$ composition with $n$ entries equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.

2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau

([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the

([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

derivations.claim: Enumeration and ordering. Choose a conjugate core beta set long enough that every runner contains a bead, and list its bottom beads $x_1<\cdots<x_e$. Take this beta length divisible by $e$. Every partition with this core has, at the same beta length, the same packed set: its packed set represents $\gamma$ and the length uniquely determines a beta-set for $\gamma$. Weight one means its total runner displacement from packing is one, so exactly one bottom bead moves down one row. Conversely each such move adds exactly $e$ boxes and preserves the core. Thus replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: the two bead lists differ by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. The new maximum is larger than both old values and the new minimum smaller than both, with the same sum. For each number of selected entries, the largest possible sum therefore does not decrease, and at least one sorted prefix increases. The sorted conjugate parts differ from these prefixes by the same beta offsets. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. For the empty core put $\gamma_i=0$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement.

Choose a lift with valuation one. If $q
e1$, its finite quantum characteristic $e$ is its multiplicative order, and is prime to the field characteristic; use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ and $\hat q=X$. The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}
e0$, so $
u([e]_X)=1$; also $
u([h]_X)=0$ when $e
mid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $
u([e]_1)=
u(p)=1$ and $
u([h]_1)=0$ for $p
mid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. This extension preserves the decomposition multiplicities because the q-Schur simple modules are absolutely irreducible and its integral Weyl modules commute with scalar extension. In both cases the generic factorial is nonzero and [F2] applies.

Restriction. If $\lambda$ is not restricted, some $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge e$, so removing the last $e$ boxes of row $i$ leaves a partition. Its size is $|\gamma|$ and its core is $\gamma$, so it equals $\gamma$. Thus $\lambda$ is obtained by adding $e$ boxes to row $i$ of $\gamma$. An $e$-core has $\gamma_r-\gamma_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$, since otherwise it has a removable horizontal $e$-strip. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property. Therefore the only nonrestricted member is $\lambda_1=(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$; it is indeed nonrestricted because its first-row difference is at least $e$.

Evaluate the balanced formula. A nonzero coefficient involves a hook of length divisible by $e$. A weight-one abacus has exactly one bead-gap pair of equal residue with the gap below the bead: $x_k+e$ and $x_k$; thus its only $e$-divisible hook has length $e$. Any surviving term in [F2] replaces two bead values, and its new runner counts equal the old ones: either $e$ divides the transfer $h_{ac}$, leaving residues fixed, or $e$ divides $h_{ab}=h_{ac}+\beta_b-\beta_c$, exchanging their residues. Hence its sorted symbol is one of the $\lambda_j$. For $j>k$, the distinct bead sets of $\lambda_k$ and $\lambda_j$ differ exactly by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. There is exactly one balanced transfer yielding this change: if $x_j<x_k+e$, its two hook lengths are $h_{ab}=e$, $h_{ac}=x_j-x_k$; if $x_j>x_k+e$, they are $h_{ab}=x_j-x_k$, $h_{ac}=e$. The difference $x_j-x_k$ is not divisible by $e$ since bottom beads are on distinct runners. Thus the respective unsigned coefficients are $+1$ and $-1$ by step 1.2. Sorting gives in either case the signed coefficient $(-1)^{j-k+1}$: in the packed core set, exactly one bead from each runner with bottom bead $>x_r$ lies between $x_r$ and $x_r+e$, so moving $x_r$ crosses $e-r$ beads; the relative sorting parity for the two moves, together with their opposite orientation, is $(-1)^{(e-j)-(e-k)+1}$. There are no other terms and no repeated contributions: the two lost and two gained bead values determine the pair and transfer uniquely. Therefore $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}]$.

Descending induction and the matrix. For $k=e$, step 2.2 gives zero on the left; all summands are actual submodule classes with nonnegative simple multiplicities, so $W^{\lambda_e}(1)=0$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. Suppose the stated rows are known for $j>k$. Substitution into step 2.2 telescopes to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Since $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ and each later term is a submodule of $W(1)$, positivity shows $W(1)\cong L^{\lambda_{k+1}}$ and $W(i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. The head quotient is $L^{\lambda_k}$, giving $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Notice that the identity $[W]=[L]+\sum_{i>0}[W(i)]$ is used only after proving all later filtration submodules vanish; it is false for a general Jantzen filtration. Reading simple multiplicities yields the complete $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix.

Specht rows. Apply the exact functor of [F4] to step 3.1 and use step 2.1: $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, while the other $D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}$ are the nonzero simples. This gives exactly the three displayed Murphy Specht class identities, hence the full $e\times(e-1)$ Murphy matrix. Conjugation sends the core to $\gamma'$ and the restricted simple labels to regular ones, and the same $\theta$ pullback applied to every module preserves all composition multiplicities. Thus the ordinary Specht matrix has the same entries under the accepted conjugate/sign label dictionary.
