4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set
of $\lambda$-tabloids; for a $\lambda$-tableau $t$ write $\{t\}$ for its
tabloid ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). The
**integral tabloid module** is the free abelian group on $\Omega_\lambda$,

$$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\mathbb Z^{(\Omega_\lambda)} =\Bigl\{\sum_{T\in\Omega_\lambda}a_T\,T:\ a_T\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{only finitely many }a_T\ne0\Bigr\},$$

with the tabloids as standard $\mathbb Z$-basis
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). The left action of $S_n$ on
tabloids extends $\mathbb Z$-linearly to $M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so that
$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is a $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-module. For every $\lambda$-tableau
$t$ put

$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma \in\mathbb Z[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\, \{\gamma\cdot t\}\in M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},$$

the **integral column polytabloid**; every coefficient lies in
$\{0,1,-1\}$ ([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).
The **integral Specht lattice** is the $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-submodule

$$S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\text{the }\mathbb Z\text{-span of } \{\,e_s:\ s\text{ a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\subseteq M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}.$$

For a commutative ring $R$ let $M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ be the free
$R$-module on the tabloids and let $S^\lambda_R\subseteq M^\lambda_R$ be the
$R$-span of the polytabloids $\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)
\{\gamma\cdot t\}$, $t$ a $\lambda$-tableau. The **standard polytabloids** are
the $e_s$ with $s$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

This item records three facts. First, the standard polytabloids form a
$\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so the integral Specht lattice has
explicit finite rank. Second, for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map
$R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}
M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\cong M^\lambda_R$ is injective onto $S^\lambda_R$: the
lattice is a direct summand of the free tabloid module and is compatible with
base change, including rings of prime characteristic. Third, for
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the module has rank one and is generated by the empty
polytabloid.

Fix a prime $p$, an integer $n\ge0$, and a **splitting $p$-modular system**
$(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$, so that $K$ and $k$ are splitting fields for
$S_n$ and its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). Write

$$M^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad S^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\subseteq M^\lambda_k$$

for the base change of the integral tabloid module and Specht lattice; the
inclusion is the injective polytabloid-span inclusion of
[[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], and $S^\lambda_k$ has the
images of the standard polytabloids as $k$-basis. Let
$\beta_k:M^\lambda_k\times M^\lambda_k\to k$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form, the unique $k$-bilinear form with orthonormal tabloid basis
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]); it is
symmetric, nondegenerate, and $S_n$-invariant.

For a $k$-subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_k$ put

$$V^{\perp}:=\{\,x\in M^\lambda_k:\beta_k(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\,\}.$$

The **form radical** of $S^\lambda_k$ is

$$R^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k\cap (S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},$$

and the **modular Specht quotient** (or James quotient) is

$$D^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda .$$

The quotient is a $k[S_n]$-module and may be zero. Its dimension is the
$p$-rank of the integral Gram matrix: if $G_\lambda$ is the Gram matrix of
$\beta$ in the standard-polytabloid basis and $\overline{G_\lambda}$ its
reduction modulo $p$, i.e. the matrix of $\beta_k$ in the standard basis of
$S^\lambda_k$, then

$$\dim_kD^\lambda=\operatorname{rank}_k\overline{G_\lambda} =\operatorname{rank}_k(G_\lambda\bmod p).$$

Everything is defined by scalar extension: $S^\lambda_k$ and $\beta_k$ are
determined by $\lambda$ and $k$, and no choice of lifts of elements of
$S^\lambda_k$ enters. $R^\lambda$ is a **form radical**, and is an
$S_n$-submodule; the identification of $R^\lambda$ with the module radical
$\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)=J(k[S_n])S^\lambda_k$
([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]) is a later consequence,
asserted only when $D^\lambda\ne0$. In particular no simplicity of
$D^\lambda$ is claimed here.

derivations.claim: The labels and their cores. The hook-length diagrams of the three partitions of $3$ are $3,2,1$ for $(3)$; $3,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second for $(2,1)$; and $3,2,1$ vertically for $(1,1,1)$. In each case there is exactly one hook of length $3$ and removing its rim hook leaves the empty partition, so all three partitions have $3$-core $\varnothing$; conversely any partition of $3$ with core $\varnothing$ is one of these, since a partition whose core has size $3$ is its own core, and $\varnothing$ has size $0=3-3$. Dominance orders them as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$.

Compute the Weyl matrix directly. First work over $\mathbb F_3$ with lift $R=\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\hat q=1$, so the only nonzero hook valuation at rank three is $v([3]_1)=1$. The conjugate beta sequence of $(3)$ is $(3,2,1)$. Its hook pairs $(3,2)$ and $(3,1)$ give the balanced sequences $(5,0,1)$ and $(4,2,0)$, of sorted shapes $(1,1,1)$ with sign $-1$ and $(2,1)$ with sign $+1$, respectively. The other pair has coefficient zero. Thus its positive sum is $[W^{(2,1)}]-[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. For $(2,1)$, beta $(4,2,0)$ and its only nonzero pair $(3,1)$ give $(5,1,0)$, shape $(1,1,1)$ with sign $+1$, so its positive sum is $[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. The column shape has no row pair and zero positive sum, hence $W^{(1,1,1)}=L^{(1,1,1)}$. Positivity and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ then show that $W^{(2,1)}(1)=L^{(1,1,1)}$ and every higher submodule is zero, giving $[W^{(2,1)}]=[L^{(2,1)}]+[L^{(1,1,1)}]$. Substitute into the first sum to get $[L^{(2,1)}]$; the same argument gives $[W^{(3)}]=[L^{(3)}]+[L^{(2,1)}]$. This proves exactly the displayed complete Weyl matrix. Scalar extension to any original field $F$ of characteristic three preserves the Weyl modules/forms and the composition series, since all Schur simple heads are absolutely simple by [F2].

Determine the specific corner images directly. The group row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ satisfies $x_{(3)}^2=6x_{(3)}$, so its rank-one Murphy form is zero in characteristic three. In the rank-one column cell the generator is $1$ and its square coefficient is $1$; the higher ideal contains $1+T_1$ and $1+T_2$ (the latter is a conjugate of the former), so this cell and its nonzero form quotient are the sign module. For the middle cell put $x=1+T_1$, $c_0=x$ and $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher row ideal. Its row symmetrizer satisfies $x_{(3)}=x+xT_2+xT_2T_1$, so $c_1T_1=-c_0-c_1$ while $c_0T_1=c_0$; and $T_2^2=1$ gives $c_0T_2=c_1$, $c_1T_2=c_0$. Thus its generator matrices are $M_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $M_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The independent cell products $x^2=2x$, $xT_2x=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$ and $xT_2^2x=2x$ give $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ over $F$. Its radical is the line $(1,-1)$; modulo it both generators act by $1$, so $D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,1)}$ is the nonzero trivial module. These two simple images are distinct since $1\ne-1$. The exact corner/form identity [F3] therefore kills precisely $L^{(3)}$ among the three labels. Projecting the Weyl matrix just proved gives all displayed Murphy Specht rows over the original $F$, without any general finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion.

Dipper-James rows and the direct group computation. Conjugating the partitions $(3)\leftrightarrow(1,1,1)$, $(2,1)\leftrightarrow(2,1)$ and applying the signed $\theta$-pullback to every Hecke module, the rows of step 3.1 become $[S^{(1,1,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]+[D^{(3)}]$ and $[S^{(3)}]=[D^{(3)}]$ in the $3$-regular labels, that is, the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ and columns $(3),(2,1)$. For the independent direct check, construct the tabloid module over $k$ using [F5]. Every middle-shape polytabloid is a difference $v_i-v_j$, and these span the two independent vectors $e_t,e_u$ displayed in [F5], so they are a basis of $S^{(2,1)}_k$. A one-row polytabloid is its unique tabloid, giving the trivial module; a one-column polytabloid is the nonzero alternating sum of all six distinct tabloids, giving the sign module. Put $w:=e_t+e_u=v_3-v_1+v_2-v_1=v_1+v_2+v_3$ in characteristic $3$: then $w\ne0$ spans a one-dimensional submodule, since $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$ gives $\sigma\cdot w=w$ for every $\sigma\in S_3$, so it realises the trivial module; and in the quotient, $(12)\cdot e_t+e_t=(v_3-v_2)+(v_3-v_1)=2v_3-v_1-v_2=3v_3-w\equiv0$ shows that $(12)$ acts by $-1$. All transpositions are conjugate and act on a one-dimensional quotient, so they all act by $-1$ and the quotient is sign. The orthonormal tabloid form has middle Gram matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in $(e_t,e_u)$; its characteristic-three kernel is $k(e_t+e_u)=kw$. Thus the James quotient $D^{(2,1)}$ is precisely this sign quotient, while the row form has norm $1$ and $D^{(3)}$ is trivial. With $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F5], and the just-computed $D^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $D^{(2,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ (the complete list is [F4]), the direct rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$, matching the matrix obtained from the Schur functor entry by entry.

replacement_item.title: The simple type-A Hecke modules are indexed by e-regular partitions
replacement_item.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.
replacement_item.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use finite joint-primary projections without presupposing which labels survive. The regular right module has a cellular filtration with quotients copies of the cells; refining their common flags in [F3] gives a simultaneous triangular flag on it. Thus each $L_a$ is annihilated by a polynomial $\prod_b(X-b)^N$, with finitely many diagonal values $b\in F$ and $N\ge\dim H$. Polynomial Bezout and the Chinese remainder construction give $p_{a,b}$ congruent to one modulo $(X-b)^N$ and zero modulo the other factors. Substituting $L_a$ gives commuting idempotents. For a joint word $\xi$, their product $P_\xi$ is idempotent in $H$ and on a cell flag has diagonal one exactly at tableaux with word $\xi$, zero elsewhere. An idempotent has zero image if and only if all these diagonal entries vanish: its triangular matrix would otherwise be nilpotent and idempotent, hence zero. The vector-space functor $M\mapsto MP_\xi$ is exact on $H$-modules, because a lift $x$ of $y=yP_\xi$ can be replaced by $xP_\xi$, and kernels are preserved. No centrality or $H$-submodule assertion for this image is needed. [F3, F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For finite $e$, equality of two diagonal values $[a]_q,[b]_q$ is equivalent to $a\equiv b\pmod e$. Indeed $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ for all integers, including negative integers. When $q\ne1$, $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$, and when $q=1$, $e=\operatorname{char}F$ and the q-integer is the integer reduced to $F$. Thus a joint word is exactly a residue word in the node convention $c-r\pmod e$. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

1.3 Prove the complete ladder-boundary comparison. Put $L(s,c)=(e-1)s+c-e$. Suppose $\alpha$ is restricted, every occupied node has $L<l$, and the addable ladder-$l$ set is nonempty. Set $C=l+e-1$, $T=\lfloor C/(e-1)\rfloor$, $d=C-(e-1)T\in\{0,\ldots,e-2\}$ and $u_s=C-(e-1)s$. For $1\le s\le T$, $0\le\alpha_s\le u_s$, and no positive row occurs beyond $T$. The deficits $h_s=u_s-\alpha_s$ are nonnegative and satisfy $h_{s+1}-h_s=\alpha_s-\alpha_{s+1}-(e-1)\le0$. An addable ladder-$l$ row has deficit zero; thereafter every deficit is zero. Consecutive such rows have width difference $e-1>0$, so the ladder addables form a terminal interval $s_0,\ldots,T$. A first equality row that is not addable simply precedes this interval. Adding its bottommost $k$ nodes therefore adds in rows $T-k+1,\ldots,T$. The length of $\alpha$ is $T$ for $d>0$ and $T-1$ for $d=0$, including the empty case $T=1,d=0$. If $\beta\unrhd\alpha$ has the same size, its length is at most that of $\alpha$, by the prefix inequality at that length. For $d=0$ all addable rows of $\beta$ are at most $T$. For $d>0$ the sole possible extra row is $T+1$, with residue $-T$, different from $i=l\bmod e=d+1-T\bmod e$ since $1\le d+1<e$. Hence every addable $i$-node of $\beta$ lies in a row at most $T$. If $\gamma$ adds any $k$ of these initial addables, at row cutoff $r$ its prefix increment is at least $\max(0,k-\max(T-r,0))$, exactly the increment for the bottommost-$k$ extension $\delta$ of $\alpha$. Adding $\beta$'s prefix inequalities proves $\gamma\unrhd\delta$. This holds for every $k$ simultaneously and needs no same-content premise. [given, construct, algebra]

1.4 The integral intersection factorization. Work over $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Suppose a row-standard tableau $t$ already agrees with $t^\eta$ on rows before $j$, and let $B$ be the canonical label interval of row $j$. In rows $r\ge j$ let $\beta_r$ count its $B$-labels. First rearrange labels inside $B$ into increasing row-reading order, then do the same with all remaining tail labels, preserving the number of labels from each interval in every row. This gives a tableau $v$ whose row $r$ consists of a $B$-segment of length $\beta_r$ followed by a tail-segment of length $\eta_r-\beta_r$. The sorting removes inversions separately within the two label intervals, so $d(t)=d(v)wa$ with additive length, $w\in S_B$, and $a$ a permutation of the remaining tail labels. The intervals are disjoint, so $T_a$ commutes with $x_B$, and $T_wx_B=Q^{\ell(w)}x_B$. Let $K'$ be the subgroup cutting each canonical row $r\ge j$ into lengths $\beta_r,\eta_r-\beta_r$, while retaining the earlier rows. Let $K$ cut $B$ into consecutive lengths $\beta_r$ and the tail into consecutive lengths $\eta_r-\beta_r$, again retaining earlier rows. The permutation $d(v)$ increases on these segments on both sides and transports $K'$ to $K$. Hence $x_{K'}T_{d(v)}=T_{d(v)}x_K$, by expansion into length-additive standard-basis words. If $E$ consists of the minimal representatives with $S_\eta=\bigsqcup_{u\in E}uK'$, then $x_\eta=\sum_{u\in E}T_ux_{K'}$. Write $\nu=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{j-1},\eta_j,\eta_j-\beta_j,\ldots,\eta_k-\beta_k)$, omitting zero parts. Multiplication of $x_K$ by $x_B$ gives $[\beta]!_Qx_\nu$: the $B$-intersection subgroup contributes $\sum Q^{\ell(b)}=[\beta]!_Q$, while its tail and earlier-row factors commute with $x_B$. Consequently the exact identity is $x_\eta T_{d(t)}x_B=Q^{\ell(w)}[\beta]!_Q\sum_{u\in E}T_uT_{d(v)}x_\nu T_a$. No scalar is divided out. Sorting $\nu$ to a partition uses the invertible block-reordering identity in [F5], so this is in $[\beta]!_Q Hx_{\nu^+}H$. If $\nu^+\ntrianglelefteq\eta$, the dominance-ideal assertion in [F5] makes its shape-$\eta$ part vanish. Otherwise the first $j+1$ largest parts of $\nu$ have sum at least $\eta_1+\cdots+\eta_j+\eta_j-\beta_j$; comparison with $\eta$ gives $\beta_j\ge\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}$. [F5, construct, algebra]

2.1 Canonical-row support without factorial cancellation. The semistandard permutation-basis theorem [[lem-type-a-hecke-permutation-modules-have-semistandard-murphy-bases-and-specht-filtrations]], followed by star, gives an exact coordinate condition for $Hx_\rho$: every supported right Murphy tableau has semistandard type $\rho$. Apply it to the factor remaining after $[\beta]!_Q$ in step 1.4, before putting back $T_a$. This factor belongs to $Hx_\nu$. In shape $\eta$, semistandardness forces the first $\eta_1$ labels into the first row, the next $\eta_2$ into the second, and so on through $B$: a label cannot occur below its own row, and each earlier row is already full. Thus its right tableaux have the first $j$ canonical rows. The permutation $a$ uses only later labels. Expanding $T_a$ by the row action and straightening cannot alter these canonical rows: their prefix counts are maximal, and same-shape straightening increases every tableau-prefix count by that supplier's Statement. This proves the canonical-row assertion even for the quotient by the displayed factorial. Starting at $j=1$, repeat steps 1.4 and 2.1 for each surviving standard-tableau term. If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$, every surviving term at that stage has $\beta_j\ge e$, so $[e]!_Q$ divides its factor $[\beta]!_Q$. Later multiplication and integral straightening preserve this common divisor. This establishes the full repeated-symmetrizer support and divisibility used below. [F5, step 1.4, algebra]

2.2 For restricted $\eta$, number its nodes by increasing $L$, taking lower rows first on a tie, to obtain $t_\eta$. Moving right increases $L$ by one and moving down by $e-1$, so it is standard. The diagrams $\alpha_l$ of nodes with $L<l$ and $\delta_l$ with $L\le l$ are restricted: their row widths are the minimum of the restricted widths of $\eta$ and the positive part of the affine cutoff bound, each having adjacent difference at most $e-1$. A node on ladder $l$ forces every lower positive position on that ladder to be occupied, since $\eta_{s+1}\ge\eta_s-(e-1)$. Thus $\delta_l$ adds the bottommost $a_l$ ladder addables to $\alpha_l$. Any competing standard tableau with the same full residue word has, in the corresponding block, $a_l$ additions all of residue $l$. Every such node was addable before the block: adding an $i$-node creates new addable corners only of residues $i+1,i-1$, distinct from $i$ for $e\ge2$. Starting with the empty diagrams, step 1.3 inductively shows its shape dominates $\delta_l$ at every completed block, and hence its final shape dominates $\eta$. No strictly lower shape has the word of $t_\eta$, and no same-shape tableau uniqueness is asserted. [step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose $P_\xi$ for the word of $t_\eta$. It has nonzero image on $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and zero image on every $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\lhd\eta$, by steps 1.2 and 2.2. Therefore it has zero image on their form quotients. Apply the exact projection to a composition series of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$. Some constituent has nonzero image; by [F1] and [F4] it is a nonzero $D_{\mathrm M}(\rho)$ with $\rho\unlhd\eta$. The exclusion forces $\rho=\eta$, proving the restricted Murphy quotient nonzero over the original field. This is a joint-word and cellular-support proof, not an import of cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 If $\eta_j-\eta_{j+1}\ge e$ for some $j$, every surviving term at that row has $\beta_j\ge e$ by steps 1.4 and 2.1 and is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Later multiplication and straightening cannot remove this polynomial factor. Every Gram entry is the coefficient of $x_\eta$ in $x_\eta T_{d(s)}T_{d(t)}^*x_\eta$ modulo higher shapes; first expand its middle factor in the row-module basis and apply the proved row calculation. Thus every entry is divisible by $[e]!_Q$. Specializing $Q$ to $q$ makes that factor zero, so the entire Murphy form vanishes and $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)=0$. This concerns a common divisor of entries, not a product-of-hooks formula for a determinant. Combining with step 3.1 proves the finite-$e$ Murphy criterion. [F1, F5, step 1.4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For $e>n$, including infinity, distinct standard tableaux of any shapes have distinct full diagonal words. At their first unequal step the preceding diagram has size $a-1$; its distinct addable-corner contents differ by a nonzero integer of absolute value at most $a\le n$, so their q-integers differ. Induction recovers every next node. Consequently every tableau word of $C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ occurs in no strictly lower cell. Exact projections as in step 3.1 and diagonal multiplicity one in [F4] show that all $\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ flag factors occur in $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$; thus this quotient has the full cell dimension and its form radical is zero. In particular at $e=\infty$ every partition is restricted and has nonzero quotient. At $n=0$ the unique cell is $F$ with norm one. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Establish the complete semisimplicity clause. Put $f_\eta=\dim C_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$ and $d_\eta=\dim D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, with zero for a zero quotient. The Murphy basis gives $\dim H=\sum_\eta f_\eta^2$. On each nonzero quotient its nondegenerate form and the cell law supply all rank-one operators. Since the cells are right modules, their action gives a surjective algebra map $H\to\operatorname{End}_F(D_{\mathrm M}(\eta))^{\mathrm{op}}$, a full matrix algebra after transpose. Its kernels are distinct maximal two-sided ideals: equality would give the same matrix-algebra simple module, contradicting [F1]. They are pairwise comaximal. Their finite product map is surjective: for each kernel $I_a$ and each other $I_b$ choose $u_{ab}\in I_b$ congruent to one modulo $I_a$, multiply over $b\ne a$, and use these elements to isolate each prescribed matrix component. Its kernel is the radical by the complete simple list and [F6]. Hence $\dim(H/\operatorname{rad}H)=\sum_\eta d_\eta^2$. Step 4.2 makes this equal to $\dim H$ when $e>n$, giving an isomorphism with a product of full matrix algebras over $F$. When finite $e\le n$, the one-dimensional Murphy row cell has norm $[n]!_q=0$, since $x_{(n)}^2=[n]!_q x_{(n)}$. Its quotient dimension is zero while its cell dimension is one; every other $d_\eta\le f_\eta$. The dimension sum is therefore strictly smaller and $\operatorname{rad}H\ne0$. This proves both directions of part 3 without any claim that some Specht module must be reducible. [F1, F5, F6, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Apply the same exact involution to every Murphy quotient: $D^\lambda=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is nonzero exactly when $\lambda'$ is restricted, equivalently when $\lambda$ is regular. The nonzero quotients remain pairwise distinct absolutely simple and complete by [F1] and [F2]. This proves parts 1 and 2, and step 5.1 gives part 3. At $q=1$, [F6] gives precisely the ordinary $p$-regular group classification, including characteristic two; no splitting or semisimplicity assumption was made. All selections and polynomial computations were finite, so no choice principle is used. [F1, F2, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

replacement_item.title: The type-A Hecke decomposition matrix is dominance unitriangular
replacement_item.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $e=e(F,q)$ and $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For
$\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$ let
$$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}],$$
the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ in a composition series of the Specht module
$S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]],
[[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu\unrhd\lambda,$$
where $\unrhd$ is the dominance order on partitions
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]): a simple factor $D^{\mu}$ of
$S^{\lambda}$ can occur only if the $e$-regular label $\mu$ dominates
$\lambda$. Equivalently the decomposition matrix $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ is
unitriangular along dominance. This constrains but does not compute the
entries: no off-diagonal decomposition number is determined by cellularity.
replacement_item.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ and simple quotients $D^{\mu}$ in the signed conjugate normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), together with the dominance order on partitions of $n$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F1] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\mu}=(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ for the conjugate partitions, where $S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module and $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$; pullback along $\theta$ is exact and preserves submodules, quotients, composition multiplicities and simplicity.

[F2] ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]) For the Murphy cellular basis of $H$ the composition multiplicity $[S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]$ satisfies $[S^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ whenever $D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$ and is zero unless $\nu\unrhd\rho$.

[F3] ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) Conjugation reverses dominance: $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ if and only if $\mu\unrhd\lambda$.

[F4] ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) $D^{\mu}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\mu$.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Invariance of composition multiplicities under the normalisation: by [F1] the twist $(-)^\theta$ is an exact equivalence of module categories with inverse $(-)^\theta$ itself, so it is additive on short exact sequences and carries composition series to composition series; hence $[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]=[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$ for all $\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 Vanishing: if $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, then $[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]\ne0$ by step 1.1, so $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ by [F2], and conjugation reversal [F3] gives $\mu\unrhd\lambda$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

2.2 Diagonal: taking $\lambda=\mu$ in step 1.1 gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Assembly: steps 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the two claims; ordering the rows and columns of $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ by any linear extension of dominance displays the unitriangular shape, and no off-diagonal entry is determined by the cellular structure. At $q=1$, [F1] and [F4] identify the same ordinary group labels; over a splitting p-modular system this agrees with [[thm-symmetric-group-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]] within that supplier's hypotheses. The present proof establishes the bound over every field. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

replacement_item.title: Virtual Weyl combinations detect q-Schur block separation
replacement_item.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S=S(d,n)$ be the
$q$-Schur algebra over $F$ with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Let $M$ be a finite
dimensional right $S$-module all of whose composition factors lie in a single
block $B$ of $S$
([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and let integers $a_{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, satisfy
$$[M]=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$$
in the Grothendieck group $G_0(S\text{-mod})$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]). Then
$W^{\lambda}$ lies in $B$ whenever $a_{\lambda}\ne0$. In particular no nonzero
virtual combination of Weyl classes all of whose terms lie outside $B$ can
equal the class of a module in $B$.

No choice principle is used.
replacement_item.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, the algebra $S=S(d,n)$ with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, a finite dimensional right $S$-module $M$ whose composition factors all lie in one block $B$, and integers $a_{\lambda}$ with $[M]=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$ in $G_0(S\text{-mod})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]).

[F1] Blocks: $1=\sum_i\epsilon_i$ is the unique decomposition of the identity of $S$ into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents, the blocks are the two-sided ideals $B_i=S\epsilon_i=\epsilon_iS$, and for every right $S$-module $N$ one has $N=\bigoplus_iN\epsilon_i$; a simple module $L$ lies in exactly one block and satisfies $L\epsilon_i=L$ for that $i$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]). We write $\epsilon_B$ for the idempotent of the block $B$ of the statement.

[F2] Each Weyl module has nonzero simple head $L^\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

[F3] The proof of [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]], steps 1.1 and 3.1, gives additive weight dimensions and the weight matrix $K_{\lambda\nu}=\dim(W^\lambda1_\nu)$. This matrix, restricted to partitions with at most $d$ parts, is unitriangular and hence invertible by [[lem-kostka-change-of-basis-is-dominance-unitriangular]]. Applying these dimensions to a zero virtual Weyl combination forces every coefficient to vanish. This proves the linear independence used here; no Weyl filtration of an arbitrary module is assumed.

[F4] An exact functor between abelian categories induces a homomorphism of Grothendieck groups, and the finite-dimensional $S$-modules form an abelian category in which $G_0$ is computed by composition multiplicities ([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Multiplication by the central idempotent $\epsilon_B$ is the projection of every right $S$-module onto its $B$-summand: $N=\bigoplus_iN\epsilon_i$ by [F1], so $N\epsilon_B$ is that direct summand and is a submodule, and $N\epsilon_B=N$ exactly when all composition factors of $N$ lie in $B$. The assignment $N\mapsto N\epsilon_B$ is exact, because it is the projection onto a direct summand of the identity functor: for $f:N\to N'$ one has $f(N\epsilon_B)=f(N)\epsilon_B$, $\ker(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\ker f)\epsilon_B$ and $\operatorname{im}(f|_{N\epsilon_B})=(\operatorname{im}f)\epsilon_B$, so it preserves kernels and images. [F1, F4]

1.2 A nonzero finite-dimensional module has a simple quotient: choose a proper submodule of maximal vector-space dimension. If a Weyl module had two nonzero summands, each would have a nonzero head, so its head would not be simple, contrary to [F2]. Thus it is indecomposable. Its block decomposition [F1] has precisely one nonzero summand, the block containing its head $L^\lambda$; hence $W^\lambda\epsilon_B$ is either $W^\lambda$ or $0$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Apply the exact projection of step 1.1 to the class identity of the hypothesis. Since $M\epsilon_B=M$ by the hypothesis that all composition factors of $M$ lie in $B$, and since $W^{\lambda}\epsilon_B$ is $W^{\lambda}$ or $0$ by step 1.2, the induced identity in $G_0$ reads $$[M]=\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\in B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}].$$ Subtracting it from the given identity $[M]=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$ yields $$\sum_{\lambda:\,W^{\lambda}\notin B}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]=0$$ in $G_0(S\text{-mod})$. [F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By the linear independence of the Weyl classes [F3], all coefficients in the vanishing combination of step 2.1 are zero: $a_{\lambda}=0$ for every $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}\notin B$, which is the contrapositive of the assertion that $a_{\lambda}\ne0$ implies $W^{\lambda}\in B$. [F3, step 2.1] ∎

replacement_item.title: q-Schur Weyl modules are in the same block iff their labels have the same e-core
replacement_item.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $n\ge0$ and $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently, for finite $e$, the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. For $e=\infty$ we set $C_\infty(\lambda):=\lambda$; the algebra is semisimple and its blocks are indexed by the partitions of $n$.

No choice principle is used.
replacement_item.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, parameter $q$, quantum characteristic $e$, integer $d\ge n$, and the Weyl modules in the statement. Write $S=S_F(d,n)$ and $W^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}_F$.

[F1] The semistandard cellular basis has cells $W^{\lambda}$, nonzero absolutely simple heads $L^{\lambda}$, and dominance-unitriangular decomposition multiplicities $d_{\lambda\mu}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The cellular anti-involution induces contragredient duality fixing the simple isomorphism classes, through the nondegenerate cell form on each simple head ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The balanced hook-ratio Jantzen formula and alternating beta symbols ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]) use conjugate beta numbers $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+N-j$, with $N$ sufficiently large, and read $$\sum_{r>0}[W^{\lambda}(r)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(v(h^{\lambda}_{ab})-v(h^{\lambda}_{ac})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}],$$ where $W^{\lambda}(r)$ are filtration submodules, $W^{\lambda}(1)=\operatorname{rad}W^{\lambda}$, and the right hand symbols are zero on repeated or negative entries and otherwise have the sign of sorting the beta sequence. The suppliers must carry this balanced form; the earlier displayed unbalanced manuscript indices do not preserve degree.

[F3] Core abaci are obtained by packing beads upwards on each runner, so their shapes depend only on runner bead counts; rim-hook removal is a bead-to-gap move ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Conjugation reverses dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]). Transposing every strip in a maximal $e$-hook removal sequence gives such a sequence for the conjugate partition; hook lengths are preserved by transposition, so its terminal core is the conjugate core. Hence $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\lambda)'$.

[F4] Primitive central idempotents decompose the identity, and every finite-dimensional module splits into their block summands ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]). Weyl classes are linearly independent in the Grothendieck group, so a nonzero accumulated Weyl coefficient in the class of a module supported in one block forces that Weyl module into the block ([[lem-virtual-weyl-combinations-detect-q-schur-block-separation]], [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]).



[F5] The radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is nilpotent and its quotient semisimple ([[thm-jacobson-radical-is-nilpotent-and-the-quotient-is-semisimple]]); the Wedderburn decomposition is a product of matrix rings over division rings ([[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]]). Cellular ideal layers are the tensor products of the contragredient left cell and the right cell ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. For $n=0$, $S_F(d,0)=F$, with its one empty-label module, so all assertions hold directly; hence assume $n>0$. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Composition-factor cores. An off-head simple occurs in $W^{\lambda}$ exactly when it occurs in its radical, equivalently in the positive Jantzen sum: the first submodule is the radical and every later one is contained in it. Its nonzero multiplicity in that sum implies it occurs in some $W^{\mu}$ with $J_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, since otherwise its coefficient in the sum would be zero. Step 2.1 gives the same core and strict dominance descent. Induction on the finite dominance poset proves that every factor $L^{\nu}$ of $W^{\lambda}$ has $C_e(\nu)=C_e(\lambda)$. No identity equating the radical class with the positive sum is asserted. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical. [F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. By [F5] and the absolute simplicity in [F1], the semisimple quotient is a product of full matrix rings over $F$. Lift its matrix diagonal idempotents: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ changes an error $a=u^2-u$ to $-3a^2+4a^3$, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_\nu$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_\nu=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda\nu}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Assume $e<\infty$. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, with $l=\ell(\gamma)$, and set $\rho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu\ne\rho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=\rho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $\nu$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $\nu$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows. [F3, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 The bridge coefficients are nonzero. Write $l=\ell(\mu)=\ell(\sigma)$. If $i>1$, then $\sigma_1=\mu_1$ and the row1 hook pair in $\nu$ at columns $j,\mu_1+1$ has lengths $A=h^{\mu}_{1j}$ and $h$: the first is nondivisible because row1 precedes the first divisible row, and the second is divisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\mu$, so its coefficient is nonzero. If $i=1$, then $\sigma_1=j-1$, and the row1 pair at columns $j,j+1$ has lengths $h,h-1$; its balanced transfer $h-1$ sorts to $\mu$, again giving a nonzero coefficient. For $\eta$, the pair at columns $1,\sigma_1+1$ has lengths $A'=\sigma_1+h+l-1$ and $h$. When $i>1$, $A'-h^{\mu}_{i1}=A$, so $A'$ is nondivisible; when $i=1$, $A'=h^{\mu}_{11}+h-1$, also nondivisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\eta$. Each claimed target has precisely two lost and two gained beta values, so the uniqueness argument in step 2.2 rules out cancellation. Thus both $J_{\nu\mu}$ and $J_{\nu\eta}$ are nonzero. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 6.1] ∎

replacement_item.title: The weight-one block decomposition pattern
replacement_item.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with finite quantum characteristic $2\le e<\infty$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), let $\gamma$ be an $e$-core of $m$, put $n=m+e$, and fix $d\ge n$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). There are exactly $e$ partitions $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$ of $n$ with $e$-core $\gamma$; list them in dominance order, $\lambda_1\rhd\lambda_2\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. In the source's (Murphy) normalisation the Weyl modules and simple modules of this weight-one class satisfy $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$ and $$[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]\qquad(1\le k<e),$$ so the decomposition matrix of the class is the $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix with rows and columns $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$. Moreover exactly $\lambda_1$ is not $e$-restricted, while $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_e$ are. Under the Schur functor ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]) the corresponding Murphy Specht classes are $$[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}],\qquad [S^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_{k+1}}_{\mathrm M}]\ (2\le k<e),\qquad [S^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}],$$ with $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$; conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to both modules ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]) gives the corresponding decomposition matrix for the page's Dipper-James Specht modules in $e$-regular labels.

No choice principle is used.
replacement_item.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with finite quantum characteristic $2\le e<\infty$, an $e$-core $\gamma$ of $m$, the integer $n=m+e$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,n)$ for $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, where $d\ge n$.

[F1] Each Weyl module has simple head $L^{\lambda}$ of multiplicity one, the decomposition matrix is dominance-unitriangular, and all simple modules are obtained this way ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). In a finite-dimensional module, a simple head implies indecomposability: any nonzero direct summand has a nonzero head, so two nonzero summands would give a nonsimple head.

[F2] The corrected balanced Jantzen formula sums positive filtration **submodules**, not their successive quotients: $$\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda}_F(i)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}_F].$$ Here $\beta_b=\lambda'_b+N-b$ for a fixed sufficiently long conjugate beta sequence, and the right hand symbols are alternating symbols: sort strictly decreasing, attach the sorting sign, and vanish on repeated or negative entries. The equal transfer preserves total size. Moreover $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$. This is the balanced hook-ratio formula required from [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Its source arithmetic must be repaired before binding: the manuscript's displayed beta indices are inconsistent, while its worked Example 5.28 determines the balanced transfer.

[F3] Core-quotient and abacus theory: a weight-one partition is obtained from a packed core abacus by moving the bottom bead of one runner down one place. The bead move removes/adds a rim $e$-hook, and distinct runners give distinct partitions ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Restricted means $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i$ ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F4] The exact Schur functor sends $W^{\lambda}$ to $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $L^{\lambda}$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, whose nonzero labels are precisely the restricted partitions. The ordinary Specht dictionary is the proved generic-$q$ form bridge and uses conjugation and the same $\theta$ pullback on every module ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Enumeration and ordering. Choose a conjugate core beta set long enough that every runner contains a bead, and list its bottom beads $x_1<\cdots<x_e$. Take this beta length divisible by $e$. Every partition with this core has, at the same beta length, the same packed set: its packed set represents $\gamma$ and the length uniquely determines a beta-set for $\gamma$. Weight one means its total runner displacement from packing is one, so exactly one bottom bead moves down one row. Conversely each such move adds exactly $e$ boxes and preserves the core. Thus replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: the two bead lists differ by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. The new maximum is larger than both old values and the new minimum smaller than both, with the same sum. For each number of selected entries, the largest possible sum therefore does not decrease, and at least one sorted prefix increases. The sorted conjugate parts differ from these prefixes by the same beta offsets. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. For the empty core put $\gamma_i=0$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement. [F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a lift with valuation one. If $q\ne1$, its finite quantum characteristic $e$ is its multiplicative order, and is prime to the field characteristic; use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ and $\hat q=X$. The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}\ne0$, so $\nu([e]_X)=1$; also $\nu([h]_X)=0$ when $e\nmid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $\nu([e]_1)=\nu(p)=1$ and $\nu([h]_1)=0$ for $p\nmid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. This extension preserves the decomposition multiplicities because the q-Schur simple modules are absolutely irreducible and its integral Weyl modules commute with scalar extension. In both cases the generic factorial is nonzero and [F2] applies. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Restriction. If $\lambda$ is not restricted, some $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge e$, so removing the last $e$ boxes of row $i$ leaves a partition. Its size is $|\gamma|$ and its core is $\gamma$, so it equals $\gamma$. Thus $\lambda$ is obtained by adding $e$ boxes to row $i$ of $\gamma$. An $e$-core has $\gamma_r-\gamma_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$, since otherwise it has a removable horizontal $e$-strip. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property. Therefore the only nonrestricted member is $\lambda_1=(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$; it is indeed nonrestricted because its first-row difference is at least $e$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Evaluate the balanced formula. A nonzero coefficient involves a hook of length divisible by $e$. A weight-one abacus has exactly one bead-gap pair of equal residue with the gap below the bead: $x_k+e$ and $x_k$; thus its only $e$-divisible hook has length $e$. Any surviving term in [F2] replaces two bead values, and its new runner counts equal the old ones: either $e$ divides the transfer $h_{ac}$, leaving residues fixed, or $e$ divides $h_{ab}=h_{ac}+\beta_b-\beta_c$, exchanging their residues. Hence its sorted symbol is one of the $\lambda_j$. For $j>k$, the distinct bead sets of $\lambda_k$ and $\lambda_j$ differ exactly by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. There is exactly one balanced transfer yielding this change: if $x_j<x_k+e$, its two hook lengths are $h_{ab}=e$, $h_{ac}=x_j-x_k$; if $x_j>x_k+e$, they are $h_{ab}=x_j-x_k$, $h_{ac}=e$. The difference $x_j-x_k$ is not divisible by $e$ since bottom beads are on distinct runners. Thus the respective unsigned coefficients are $+1$ and $-1$ by step 1.2. Sorting gives in either case the signed coefficient $(-1)^{j-k+1}$: in the packed core set, exactly one bead from each runner with bottom bead $>x_r$ lies between $x_r$ and $x_r+e$, so moving $x_r$ crosses $e-r$ beads; the relative sorting parity for the two moves, together with their opposite orientation, is $(-1)^{(e-j)-(e-k)+1}$. There are no other terms and no repeated contributions: the two lost and two gained bead values determine the pair and transfer uniquely. Therefore $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}]$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Descending induction and the matrix. For $k=e$, step 2.2 gives zero on the left; all summands are actual submodule classes with nonnegative simple multiplicities, so $W^{\lambda_e}(1)=0$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. Suppose the stated rows are known for $j>k$. Substitution into step 2.2 telescopes to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Since $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ and each later term is a submodule of $W(1)$, positivity shows $W(1)\cong L^{\lambda_{k+1}}$ and $W(i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. The head quotient is $L^{\lambda_k}$, giving $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Notice that the identity $[W]=[L]+\sum_{i>0}[W(i)]$ is used only after proving all later filtration submodules vanish; it is false for a general Jantzen filtration. Reading simple multiplicities yields the complete $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix. [F1, F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Specht rows. Apply the exact functor of [F4] to step 3.1 and use step 2.1: $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, while the other $D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}$ are the nonzero simples. This gives exactly the three displayed Murphy Specht class identities, hence the full $e\times(e-1)$ Murphy matrix. Conjugation sends the core to $\gamma'$ and the restricted simple labels to regular ones, and the same $\theta$ pullback applied to every module preserves all composition multiplicities. Thus the ordinary Specht matrix has the same entries under the accepted conjugate/sign label dictionary. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎
